item.title: Unusual bird spotted on Guam ahead of Typhoon Champi
item.description: A day before Typhoon Champi put Guam in Condition of Readiness 1, what Jessica Laguaña mistook for a chicken ended up being a rare sighting of an Australasian swamphen. Laguaña was driving in Ordot to check on her in-laws when she noticed the bird near their driveway. Its striking blue-purple feathers caught her attention, prompting her to take a photo.
item.content:encoded:
A day before Typhoon Champi put Guam in Condition of Readiness 1, what Jessica Laguaña mistook for a chicken ended up being a rare sighting of an Australasian swamphen.

Laguaña was driving in Ordot to check on her in-laws when she noticed the bird near their driveway. Its striking blue-purple feathers caught her attention, prompting her to take a photo.

“I was so captivated by the blue on its chest. The bird was coming up the driveway, and it seemed like it wasn’t afraid of me. I walked by it, and it just kept going up the driveway.” Laguaña said her father-in-law leaves bird feed for the local birds in the area, and that it might have been around the area before. She said her father-in-law had seen the bird a few times prior to Typhoon Champi.

The bird’s bright red bill and oversized red frontal shield also distinguish it from Guam’s pulattat bird, or common morehen.

Avian biologist Martin Kastner said the bird can be confidently identified as the Australasian swamphen, although a similar-looking black-backed swamphen cannot be ruled out completely.

Swamphens are generally sedentary, but can disperse between islands. Kastner said the bird’s appearance on Guam is unusual, and it remains unclear whether more will be seen.

“So if this is the only bird on island, which is possible, then we might not see them very often, and it could be a one-off,” Kastner said.

Guam has no known subfossil records of its own due to the cave damage on Guam during the war. However, swamphen subfossils have been found on Rota and Tinian, suggesting the birds may have once inhabited the Marianas.

The nearest population is in Palau, where a rare endemic subspecies known as the Uek lives in marshes and taro patches and its protected by local custom.

For now, the swamphen’s origins remain a mystery. Kastner said it will be interesting to see whether any more appear on Guam.

item.content:encoded:
Typhoon In-Fa remained on track to pass about 180 miles north of Saipan and about 300 miles north of Guam on Friday, according to the Joint Typhoon Warning Center.

On Tuesday afternoon, In-Fa was located at 14.3 degrees north latitude and 162.2 degrees east longitude, more than 1,100 miles east of Guam. It was a Category 3 storm with winds of 125 mph, and was moving to the west-northwest at 2 mph.

Forecasters with the National Weather Service said In-Fa was expected to make a slight turn toward the west and increase in forward speed through Wednesday, then turn back to the west-northwest.

The storm was expected to begin intensifying on Wednesday night.

Typhoon winds extended out 35 miles from the center of the storm, with tropical storm-force winds extending 90 miles from the center.

item.title: CNMI delegate urges path forward as DHS halts Chinese travel program
item.description: Emphasizing that the program has been "suspended, not terminated," CNMI Del. Kimberlyn King-Hinds said Tuesday she is working with federal officials to address concerns that prompted the suspension of a key travel program for Chinese visitors to the Northern Mariana Islands. King-Hinds said she spoke directly with the White House, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and House leadership f
item.content:encoded:
Emphasizing that the program has been "suspended, not terminated," CNMI Del. Kimberlyn King-Hinds said Tuesday she is working with federal officials to address concerns that prompted the suspension of a key travel program for Chinese visitors to the Northern Mariana Islands.

King-Hinds said she spoke directly with the White House, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and House leadership following the Department of Homeland Security's announcement suspending the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands Economic Vitality and Security Travel Authorization Program, or EVS-TAP. She said Mullin assured her that DHS would work directly with the CNMI to better understand and address the issues that led to the suspension.

King-HInds said, "We have experienced interruptions to travel programs serving the Commonwealth before, and we will work through this together with our federal partners to address the concerns that have been raised and find a path forward, just as we have done before."

According to the delegate, the program was established with safeguards allowing DHS to suspend operations when security or law enforcement concerns arise. She said federal and local officials would work together to address those concerns and support the program's resumption as quickly as possible.

The congresswoman also warned that a lengthy suspension could further burden the Commonwealth's struggling tourism sector.

"Our tourism industry is already facing tremendous challenges, and a prolonged disruption would have serious consequences for our businesses, workers and families," King-Hinds said. "We must also consider the immediate effects on airlines, travel arrangements, and the businesses that depend on visitor arrivals."

The Department of Homeland Security announced Tuesday that it will suspend EVS-TAP effective Oct. 30, requiring Chinese nationals seeking to visit the CNMI for business or tourism to obtain a U.S. visa unless another lawful exception applies.

Chinese nationals already admitted under the program may remain through their authorized period of stay.

In a Federal Register notice, DHS said the program's suspension was warranted because of national security, immigration enforcement and law enforcement concerns. The agency cited the risk of unauthorized travel beyond the CNMI, potential espionage activities involving sensitive military infrastructure in the Mariana Islands, birth tourism concerns and previous criminal cases involving the smuggling of Chinese nationals from the CNMI to Guam.

EVS-TAP took effect in February 2025 and allowed pre-screened nationals of the People's Republic of China to travel directly to the CNMI without first obtaining a U.S. visa. More than 3,000 Chinese nationals used the program during fiscal year 2025, according to DHS.

While acknowledging that some CNMI businesses have relied on Chinese tourism, DHS said economic considerations do not outweigh what it described as acute national security, immigration and law enforcement concerns. The agency noted that Chinese visitors may still travel to the CNMI through the standard U.S. visa process.

King-Hinds said her immediate focus is ensuring the concerns identified by federal officials are addressed so the program can resume.

item.title: Southwest flood damage estimates are hundreds of millions for New Mexico alone
item.description: Intense rainstorms linked to a very active El Niño-driven Pacific hurricane season have left thousands of people in the Four Corners states displaced or facing massive cleanups from flooding. The adjoining states of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Arizona all saw substantial flooding last week, and damage assessments are just starting to trickle in from cities, towns and some of the most remote ter
item.content:encoded:
Intense rainstorms linked to a very active El Niño-driven Pacific hurricane season have left thousands of people in the Four Corners states displaced or facing massive cleanups from flooding.

The adjoining states of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Arizona all saw substantial flooding last week, and damage assessments are just starting to trickle in from cities, towns and some of the most remote territory in the continental U.S.

The northern New Mexico city of Farmington was hit particularly hard after torrential rains fell on the San Juan mountains in Colorado, sending floodwaters down the San Juan River that passes through Farmington on its way to Lake Powell on the Utah-Arizona border.

Small towns all along the river, from Pagosa Springs, Colorado, to Bloomfield, New Mexico and Bluff, Utah all saw historic flooding and are now assessing recovery challenges.

About 46,000 people live in Farmington, long a center for coal, oil and natural gas production. It's also an important hub for the northeast side of the Navajo reservation, which sprawls across three states.

Farmington residents started getting evacuation notices on their phones as early as Wednesday night.

"My sister was notified on Thursday that she had to get out," said Connie Gooch, who has lived in Farmington for more than 65 years.

Gooch's sister owns a house in a suburban neighborhood near the San Juan River.

"Every year she goes through this," Gooch said. "The river starts rising, and she starts making sandbags to put around. But this year it was so fast she didn't have time to do that."

According to National Weather Service data from a river gauge in Farmington , the San Juan grew 13 times larger in just 36 hours, late last week.

In the wee hours of Thursday morning, the river was about 3.5 feet high. By Friday, it was 14 feet high, flooding neighborhoods across the city, and possibly setting a record for the highest water ever recorded in the city.

This even after the Navajo Reservoir upstream from Farmington was able to mostly contain water rushing down from the mountains. But downstream of the reservoir, flood surges into the city came from two normally dry tributaries, Gobernador Canyon and Cañon Largo.

"This is a catastrophic flood of historic proportions," said Devon Neeley, San Juan County's public information officer.

"This river got wider than we have ever seen it in our lifetimes."

Similar reports are coming in from the other side of the San Juan mountains in Colorado.

"It's nothing like most of us have seen before," said Tyler Schmidt, captain of the fire and rescue team in the small town of South Fork, Colo. on the banks of the Rio Grande. "We had several neighborhoods that were under two to three feet of water."

Colorado Public Radio's Dan Boyce reports that responders' immediate priorities are lifting final evacuation orders as waters recede. Damaged bridges need to be assessed. Well water all down the Rio Grande's path in the San Luis valley needs to be tested.

Other drinking water impacts from the storm include sewage spills from flooded treatment plants in Sedona, Arizona and other locations. KNAU reports extensive damage on the Hopi reservation.

The Hopi reservation is surrounded by the Navajo reservation, where there have also been reports of rescues, washed out roads and flooding of historic proportions.

San Juan County, New Mexico's Neeley said fire crews, police officers, National Guard troops, and even out-of-state swift water teams rescued between 200 and 300 county residents.

"We have pulled people out of vehicles stuck in running washes. We have pulled people by helicopter off of rooftops," Neeley said. "We have used not only high-clearance vehicles from the National Guard, but amphibious vehicles because the water is so high. It's been a lot."

By Sunday, the rain had eased, river levels were falling, and some residents started returning home to assess flood damage.

Connie Gooch delivered tarps and other materials to her sister's house.

"The river was up four feet in her house," she said.

She found a neighborhood full of people moving furniture out of their homes and piling demolition debris in their front yards.

"There were trucks and cars all over the place," Gooch said. "There was a guy in front of me carrying a loaded trailer full of sheet rock that they'd chipped out of somebody's house."

But officials want the thousands of evacuated residents to stay out for now.

"The public is anxious to get back in; we recognize that, we're sympathetic to that," said San Juan County Fire Chief David Vega at a public briefing Sunday. "Now that the swift water component is out of the way, that exposes a whole new set of hazards for us," Vega added.

Public officials are concerned about hazards like raw sewage and damaged gas lines, live power lines, and the floodwater itself.

"The water is not healthy," Vega said. "Stay out of the water. Gas, diesel, pesticides, fertilizer, these are not things that you want on your clothes."

item.title: Israel's election has a high turnout, lifting opposition hopes of beating Netanyahu
item.description: Updated October 28, 2026 at 8:36 AM ChST Israeli voters turned out in their highest numbers in more than two decades in a tense national election on Tuesday to decide whether to stick with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition or change course.
item.content:encoded:
Updated October 28, 2026 at 8:36 AM ChST

Israeli voters turned out in their highest numbers in more than two decades in a tense national election on Tuesday to decide whether to stick with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition or change course.

Netanyahu is in a tight race with his top rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff, according to early exit polls after voting ended at 10 p.m. local time. The preliminary results broadcast across Israeli TV networks didn't show a clear winner, but appeared to give the opposition bloc of parties led by Eisenkot a slight edge over Netanyahu's governing coalition.

Still, the final vote count may not be known until Wednesday. And even then, if no bloc wins an outright majority, it may take days or weeks to find who will be Israel's next prime minister as party leaders try to assemble a governing coalition.

Israelis consider this one of their most consequential votes in history — the first parliamentary election since the October 2023 Hamas-led attack and the start of wars in Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East.

The early exit polls suggested Netanyahu's Likud Party won the most seats, with Eisenkot's Yashar party coming second, but no party won an outright majority in the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.

The final results will depend on the math and negotiations among broader alliances. The bloc of four opposition parties led by Eisenkot appeared to win a combined 52 seats, over the Netanyahu coalition's 50, according to three major exit polls.

Opposition leaders quickly reacted to the preliminary results, saying they suggested voters dealt a blow to Netanyahu's coalition .

Shira Efron, an analyst at the Rand Corp. think tank, agreed that it could be an opposition victory.

"This is a very good outcome for Eisenkot" and his recently formed party, Efron told NPR. "The most likely scenario is that he will receive the mandate from the president to form the government," she told NPR. She said he could try to form a minority government or join an alliance with Arab politicians.

The Central Elections Committee said 77.7% of voters cast ballots as of 10 p.m. — the highest turnout since 1999.

Enthusiasm was especially high among voters seeking to replace Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, with almost two decades in office across multiple tenures.

" Important is an underestimation, because it's much more than important. It's crucial," voter Naama Aaronsohn said of the election. "I'm worried. ... What's going to become of our country if there's not a major change?"

Another voter, Itamar Ariel, said there are problems in Israel but no one can replace Netanyahu. He said his choice is about security for Israel.

Netanyahu voiced alarm throughout the day, in a number of social media posts, commenting on the high number of Arab citizens of Israel who were turning up at the polls. Netanyahu urged his right-wing supporters to vote.

Nur Abu Na, a 30-year-old nurse, called Netanyahu's government racist against Arab citizens and said she believes it's important for the her Arab community to vote. There are two predominantly Arab parties in the elections.

"This government it's not good for us and ... not good for anyone," she said.

President Trump publicly endorsed Netanyahu . After going to war together against Iran, in June 2025 and again this February, the two leaders plan to launch major attacks against Iran after the Israeli and U.S. midterm elections.

This is a developing story and may be updated.

Daniel Estrin reported from Tel Aviv, Israel. Ruth Sherlock reported from Jerusalem. Samantha Balaban, Itay Stern, Shir David and Alon Avital contributed reporting in Israel.

item.title: A judge halted D.C. golf course renovations. Trump says they'll still start next month
item.description: After weeks of tense hearings and late-night court filings, a federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from making any further alterations to East Potomac Park, the municipal D.C. golf course that the president wants to redevelop into a championship-level venue. item.content:encoded:
After weeks of tense hearings and late-night court filings, a federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from making any further alterations to East Potomac Park, the municipal D.C. golf course that the president wants to redevelop into a championship-level venue.

The long-simmering legal battle kicked into high gear in recent weeks, after the government cut down 430 trees on the golf course with less than a day's notice. That prompted a pair of lengthy court hearings that at times turned heated, with government officials repeatedly insisting that the tree-clearing was unrelated to the renovations President Trump had touted on social media. They contradicted the president's own social media posts from that very morning by saying there was no final plan for those renovations at all.

"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president," U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote in her 70-page opinion . "And yet, here we are."

Reyes extended what was initially a two-week halt to tree removal, ordering the government not to cut down "or substantially prune or otherwise damage or impair" any trees at East Potomac Park without a court order. She also ordered it to provide "no less than ten business days' written advance notice" before closing or making any "irreversible modification" to any parts of the park while the legal battle plays out.

"By issuing this preliminary injunction, the Court does not end the round: it simply marks the ball until the parties can fully and fairly litigate this case," Reyes wrote.

Monday's ruling is a win for the D.C. Preservation League and a pair of local golfers who sued to prevent renovations earlier this year — and for the growing grassroots movement to protect the municipal course and the surrounding recreational area, which is beloved by runners, cyclists, birders and others.

"We are grateful the court intervened to stop the Trump-Vance administration's greed and lawlessness while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court," said Skye Perryman, the president of the nonprofit Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs.

In a Truth Social post late Monday, Trump said the Department of the Interior will appeal the ruling. NPR has reached out to the Department of Interior but did not hear back in time for publication.

Trump also doubled down on his earlier announcement that construction will begin on Nov. 15 and keep the park closed for 15 months, adding that the "judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project."

"To have to give advanced notices to a judge who has no expertise in Golf, Architecture, Landscaping, Construction, or anything else having to do with building such a World Class Project, is not fair, appropriate, or Constitutional," Trump wrote.

Reyes herself has said she is not interested in policing the federal government's landscaping efforts.

That's why, as she explained in Monday's opinion, she repeatedly declined to intervene in the case — instead issuing repeated warnings against any unannounced major alterations — until "the Government did what it assured all it would not do."

"The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" Reyes concluded. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."

On Tuesday afternoon, Reyes made a record of Trump's post and gave the government about 24 hours to clarify whether a plan exists to close East Potomac in mid-November and, if so, "how that can be reconciled" with what its lawyers previously told the court. She said she will schedule a status hearing for either Friday or Monday.

Reyes' strongly-worded 70-page opinion came exactly a week after a seven-hour hearing in which she clashed repeatedly with the government's lawyers. She had already rejected the administration's request to recuse herself from the case because of alleged bias.

Last week's hearing featured sworn testimony from several officials from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, to provide a fuller account of the origins and purpose of the controversial tree-clearing. But it teed up bigger questions about whether the administration had misled the court and the public over its intentions for the golf course.

"This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more," Reyes wrote on Monday. "It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."

Much of Reyes' opinion examines the gap between what Trump has said publicly and what his administration has told the court.

The most notable: Trump posted online the morning of last week's hearing that work would begin on the golf course "immediately." But hours later, in the courtroom, administration officials said in sworn testimony that they were not aware of any final plan.

Weaving together timelines and testimonies, Reyes ultimately agreed with plaintiffs that there does seem to be a golf course renovation plan (they refer to it as the "Washington National Plan") despite the administration's repeated denials.

"To be sure, the Court cannot pinpoint the exact date at which the Plan became final," Reyes wrote. "But it determines without hesitation that it occurred at some point well before October 15, 2026."

She doesn't accept the government's explanation that it cleared hundreds of healthy, non-invasive trees on such short notice to enact vegetation recommendations from a 2019 National Park Service Report (whose other recommendations, including for the city's other two municipal golf courses, went largely unaddressed in the last seven years). She called that justification "pretextual."

She took particular aim at the credibility of one witness, Gregory Wischer — a deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department — who was photographed carrying rolled-up concept plans while accompanying Trump and golf course architect Tom Fazio on a tour of East Potomac in June.

"Yet Wischer maintains that he — as Deputy Chief of Staff to the Secretary of the Interior — just spontaneously became interested in tree and vegetation management. In mid September. At the East Potomac Golf Course," Reyes wrote.

Reyes said the government "has made no compelling factual rebuttal." At one point, the administration accused the plaintiffs of conjecture "based on a handful of tweets." Reyes shut that down in Monday's opinion.

"The 'handful of tweets' are not complaints about the Red Sox's latest blown lead in the ninth. They are statements from the President of the United States, and from the Secretary of the Interior, about actions within their purview," she wrote. "And the posts say, in no uncertain terms, that a plan exists and that construction will start imminently — one even contains a final schematic of the Course's redesign."

Trump said as recently as Monday night that he believes the renovations do not require approval. But, as Reyes pointed out in her opinion, administration officials acknowledged in a July hearing that major renovations would require federal environmental and historic preservation reviews.

Last week, however, administration lawyers presented an "alternative argument" that the renovations actually cannot be reviewed under the Administrative Procedure Act.

"It says, Emily Litella-style: 'Never mind,'" Reyes wrote, referring to the perpetually about-facing Saturday Night Live character . "But parties cannot change course whenever and however the evidence suits them … And so the Court does not credit this new argument."

Plaintiffs in the lawsuit argue that the government is purposefully approaching the golf course renovations as smaller projects — like dumping debris from the White House East Wing demolition last year or cutting down hundreds of trees this month — to avoid federally required environmental reviews.

item.title: Filmmaking is 'our weapon against intolerance,' say 'La Bola Negra' directors
item.description: La Bola Negra, a new movie by Spanish filmmakers Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi — known collectively as "Los Javis" — is an epic story that takes viewers through three timelines: a young man blackballed for being gay 1932; a soldier from 1937 who falls in love with the wounded enemy prisoner; and a contemporary writer who inherits something from a grandfather he never knew, which ties the three
item.content:encoded:
La Bola Negra, a new movie by Spanish filmmakers Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi — known collectively as "Los Javis" — is an epic story that takes viewers through three timelines: a young man blackballed for being gay 1932; a soldier from 1937 who falls in love with the wounded enemy prisoner; and a contemporary writer who inherits something from a grandfather he never knew, which ties the three stories together.

"We don't have that many movies or books about the history that connects us as a community, the queer community," Ambrossi says. "That's why we wanted to make it big. We wanted to make it epic and we wanted to make it bold."

The film is based on four pages of a play that famed Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca began writing about a young man who was subject to the "black ball system" that was popular in the private clubs of 1930s Spain. Members dropped balls into a box to decide who would belong: A white ball meant you were in, a black ball meant that you were out.

But in 1936, before Lorca could finish the play, he was arrested and murdered. In order to complete Lorca's script, Calvo and Ambrossi immersed themselves in his world. "We read letters. … We were following the clues," Ambrossi says. "We were like detectives." Calvo adds, "It was fun to discover that he would like to talk about his projects in parties."

Calvo says the film helps them feel closer to a generation of gay men who came before them: "We are all connected by this black ball that we all share, that we pass to each other, every generation, a black ball, that is silence, pain, shame, but also it's a spark of life and desire and love and joy. I feel like it made me feel proud of my community and of the brave people that fought before me."

Los Javis won the prize for best directing at the Cannes Film Festival in May. La Bola Negra has been acquired by Netflix. It's in select theaters now and will begin streaming on Netflix on Dec. 2.

On the cabaret girls, or "cupletistas," who performed in Madrid in the early 20th century (portrayed by Penélope Cruz in the film)

Calvo: This generation, they thought they were going to be free forever but then two dictatorships came and they were persecuted, they were murdered, they disappeared. And it's shocking to understand that today almost no one remembers them. They were kind of lost in history. … It was shocking to feel the parallelism with the society we live in now, in which we think we could be free forever, like we're going to be free forever, we conquered the rights, we're here. But history repeats itself. Fascism is rising and it's a worrying thing and our weapon against intolerance and hate is our writing and making movies and this is what we're here to do.

On the line in the film likening a gay man's heart to an "ocean of secrets"

Ambrossi: That's not very poetic, because it's a tribute to Titanic. So it was more like a wink to the audience. The people that know, know. … Besides the Titanic tribute, we wanted to do a poetic movie. Because I think poetry is the opposite of fascism. Because poetry is full of meanings for everyone, and it's polysemic and poetry everyone will understand differently.

On feeling whole through their creative collaboration

Calvo: [I felt it] from the first play. … And since then it's been like a really natural collaboration. Today we were ... in the car talking about the next project and we're getting excited about the things we want to talk about.

It's kind of a mystery how we really are connected, like connected brains. ... Even in an interview, I know when he has to talk, I know when I have to talk, when he wants to intervene. It's a true connection.

Ambrossi: From the first day, it's weird and mysterious. And I think it's because we are so different. … I'm very emotional and I love to work with atmospheres and Javi is very detailed and specific. And also we are different, like, in our souls.

On becoming too enmeshed and breaking up during the making of the movie

Ambrossi: We were friends, then we became a romantic couple for 13 years. Then we broke up because it was unhealthy. It was like we needed to find ourselves. …

Calvo: You need to be honest as an artist. And we had a mature conversation. We said, let's move on and let's write. Let's keep on directing this movie in an honest and cathartic way.

Ambrossi: And when you're writing a movie about paying tribute to the people that came before you in the LGBTQ+ community and about how our rights are based on their suffering, it's like I just need at least to try to be happy, and we weren't happy in that relationship. So we changed.

Ann Marie Baldonado and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.
